content:
Yes, I have looked at quite a bit of Tau Ceti, and I made a technical comment in another message.

But I have a more fundamental philosophical problem. Perhaps this is something we should discuss elsewhere, but since you have such extensive experience with Lean, I would be very interested in your view.
Background:

Until April 2026, I had assumed that Mathlib4 was being built slowly and painstakingly by enthusiastic volunteers, and that only once this work had been completed (formalising the bulk of standard mathematics in Lean) would the LLMs be able to get started.
It simply never occurred to me that LLMs could formalise standard results themselves. Autoformalisation had arrived.
At the conference, https://www.icmat.es/congresos/2026/AIMD/program.php, it was explained that one needs to know enough Lean to ensure that the central theorems and the associated definitions are correct. The LLM then does the rest (but only the latest and most capable models).
There is now even Trellis https://github.com/wpegden/trellis, which does this automatically.

The «philosophical» question:

How much trust can one reasonably place in such a «Lean certificate»? By this I mean a development for which print axioms shows only the expected axioms, no sorries, and whose proof-checking infrastructure relies on tools such as con-leche or lean4lean, when those tools themselves are partly or entirely LLM-generated.

My concern is not whether Lean can verify the individual proofs once the formalisation has been produced. If Lean's kernel checks a proof term, that part is genuinely machine-checked. The more fundamental question is whether the formalisation itself faithfully represents the intended mathematical statement and definitions.

For example, how can we be sure that an LLM-generated formalisation of Sobolev spaces, or of some other standard mathematical concept, actually corresponds to the mathematical notion we intended to formalise? An LLM may produce code which is internally consistent and fully accepted by Lean, while nevertheless formalising a slightly different, weaker, or otherwise unintended statement.

This seems to me to be a different and weaker kind of certification from the situation in which the definitions and mathematical framework have themselves been carefully established and reviewed by mathematicians, and Lean is then used to verify the subsequent proofs.

This is the point that makes me hesitate about using Tau Ceti.

Uwe Brauer said:

How much trust can one reasonably place in such a «Lean certificate»? By this I mean a development for which print axioms shows only the expected axioms, no sorries, and whose proof-checking infrastructure relies on tools such as con-leche or lean4lean, when those tools themselves are partly or entirely LLM-generated.

If a proof passes comparator (which basically "prevents cheating" and which one should include in a large scale autoformalisation), it is very very likely that the Lean statement has a correct proof. In theory, a proof could still abuse a kernel bug but afaik this has never happened in a serious manner so far and probably very hard to do at this point.

Using comparator, one can also see all definitions (downstream of mathlib) needed to state the main theorem in a single, usually relatively short, file. So one has to check relatively little; provided one trusts mathlib (which there is little reason not to imo).

But as you said; it could be that the Lean statement diverges from the intended, mathematical statement.

There is no easy solution to this problem. The formal conjectures repository tracks the statements of open mathematical conjectures and misformalisations (i.e. lean def written down wrongly) unfortunately happens quite often; despite each statement carefully being checked by a reviewer. There are also quite a lot of papers on this very topic (misformalisations).

However; if a good faith actor proves some big theorem in Lean; by doing the proof you will usually catch initial misformalisations. Also as @Heath Sanchez ☉ said one can try to show equivalences, examples etc. That will bring you quite far.
In particular, when formalizing some complicated definition (say Soboloev spaces), one builds up many API lemmas, i.e. easy properties which can then be used as small steps in more complicated proofs. A misformalisation is very unlikely to survive in enough of those. AFAIK Tau Ceti also does this. So if you have say 5000 lines of code in tau ceti about Sobolev spaces and a significant amount of classic properties and characterisations are proved about them; I would not worry for the definition to be wrong (or at least not much more worried as if it had been formlized by a human)

From experience, top level LLMs (i.e. GPT 6 or Opus 5.5) by now do not make more mistakes formlising definitions than an average human would make (but they complement each other very well :)).

That being said; it is still important for standard mathematical concepts/definitions to be formalised by humans, for example to decide what is "the right generality" as well as what formalisation will be convenient to deal with

Hot take: the top models now are better at formalising definitions than humans. I asked a model 6 months ago to define Hilbert modular forms and it was a disaster. I asked one a month ago and it was perfect.

Also, models found mistakes in our very careful human-written human-reviewed formalisation of 50 Annals statements (before we went public) and in every case the LLM was correct.

I totally agree that proving all the right API is the best check on a definition but I am far less concerned about this sort of issue than I was a couple of months ago.
6 messages were moved here from #mathlib4 > Sobolev spaces (and formalization done by Armstrong and Kemp by Kevin Buzzard.
@Uwe Brauer we've drifted a lot from Sobolev spaces so I moved the conversation (which has been had many times before on this Zulip) to a more appropriate channel.

Strictly speaking, the only thing we can conclude from “this formal proof compiles in Lean” is that the code compiled in Lean. Just like any software, computers are great at doing what we tell them, not what we want, and people are really bad at telling computers what we want. For example, based on what I’ve read from the people deciphering the NS artifacts, it seems like what the OpenAI result ultimately told us is that we asked the question wrong.

In the quotation below "This" refers to earlier discussion regarding trusting a Lean certificate of a mathematical statement as a 'proper' (my quotes) formalization of a result.

Uwe Brauer said:

This seems to me to be a different and weaker kind of certification from the situation in which the definitions and mathematical framework have themselves been carefully established and reviewed by mathematicians, and Lean is then used to verify the subsequent proofs.

I imagine it is weaker because you don't understand Lean as a modelling language yet. I see the same concern applying to an informal attempt at formalizing a model in 'natural' language. I would think that because I understand (heh) the conventions in formalizing from reading papers, that I could convince myself that the paper did/did not do a good job in setting up the model.

The fact that there is a virtual machine which checks the mechanical parts of a formalization to verify a formal proof is valid is the advantage Lean has over the current system. However much you might trust (or not) the science behind the technology, trust comes from experience: you have many people trying this process and finding whether it works or not, so that trust (from a collective of the process) is developed: on the individual level, you keep writing and running tests to see if the system performs the way you want.

When it comes to trust, I think experience is more convincing than reasoned argument. (Warning: don't think too heavily on the previous sentence.)
